problem: Let $u=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $w=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ be vectors such that $u\,⊥\,v.$ Find $(v+w)\cdot u+v\cdot (u+w).$

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Dot Products Using Orthogonal Vectors
examples.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044739/assets/61cb89adc9a0cce6a434c41be5d2d1799e01e94bebe1b4f44d48bc011c1a349b.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044739/assets/00af13e5017635a0b333ecd5fc2bfc761c9612427b8a3986ba48fa904ff2eed0.png) be vectors such that $\mathbf{u} \!\perp\! \mathbf{w}$. Find $(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}+ \mathbf{w}).$
examples.worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are orthogonal vectors, we have that $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}=0$. Therefore, using linearity of the dot product to expand the parentheses, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(u+v)\cdot w+u\cdot (v+w) & =u\cdot w+v\cdot w+u\cdot v+u\cdot w \\  & =0+v\cdot w+u\cdot v+0 \\  & =v\cdot w+u\cdot v \\  & =(2\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot 3+4\cdot 1) \\  & +((-1)\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-3)+5\cdot 4)\, \\  & =(-2-9+4)+(-2+6+20) \\  & =-7+24 \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Let $u=[\begin{aligned}k \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $v=[\begin{aligned}3k \\ -6 \\ k \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ be vectors such that  $u⊥v.$ Find the value of $k.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal vectors, we have that their dot product is equal to zero.
First, let's calculate the dot product in terms of $k$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4} \\  & =k\cdot 3k+1\cdot (-6)+3\cdot k+(-2)\cdot 0 \\  & =3{k}^{2}-6+3k+0 \\  & =3({k}^{2}+k-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the dot product to zero, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3({k}^{2}+k-2) & =0 \\ 3(k+2)(k-1) & =0 \\ k & =-2,1.\end{aligned}
$$
